report:
## Conclusion: The claim is TRUE, not false

The evidence strongly supports that abaloparatide reduces vertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. This is not a false health claim—it is well-established by high-quality clinical trial data and regulatory approval.

**Key evidence:**

1. **Pivotal RCT (ACTIVE trial):** The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 ACTIVE trial found that subcutaneous abaloparatide significantly reduced new vertebral fractures compared to placebo over 18 months, with a relative risk reduction of 86% (p<0.001) ([JAMA](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640); [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27533157/?dopt=Abstract)). The absolute risk reduction was 3.6% ([managedcaremag.com](https://www.managedcaremag.com/news/fda-approves-tymlos-osteoporosis-postmenopausal-women/)).

2. **FDA approval:** The FDA approved abaloparatide (Tymlos) specifically based on this fracture-reduction evidence, indicating it for postmenopausal women at high fracture risk ([FDA label](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/208743lbl.pdf); [FDA Drug Trial Snapshot](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-approvals-and-databases/drug-trial-snapshot-tymlos)).

3. **Independent meta-analysis:** A network meta-analysis confirmed abaloparatide reduces vertebral, nonvertebral, and wrist fracture risk versus placebo and other treatments ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30953114/)).

4. **Long-term follow-up (ACTIVExtend):** Continued benefit was observed when patients transitioned to alendronate after abaloparatide, with sustained low vertebral fracture rates ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31674644/)).

**Bottom line:** Multiple independent, high-quality sources—including a randomized controlled trial published in JAMA, FDA regulatory review, and meta-analyses—consistently and robustly confirm that abaloparatide reduces vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal osteoporosis. There is no credible evidence contradicting this claim; it should be considered well-supported, not false.
